explanations.american-revolutionary-war--french-revol: The French Revolution's own article, at the revision this atlas cites for that record, says: **"At the same time, the American Revolution and the European revolts of the 1780s inspired public debate on issues such as patriotism, liberty, equality, and democracy."** The sentence names the American Revolution, the broader movement; this atlas holds its armed phase, which the war's own article calls **"the final eight years of the broader American Revolution"** (revision 1376266742). That identification is the one step this edge takes beyond the article, and it is why the type is `inspired` and the confidence `probable`: the sentence names an inspiration among others and asserts no more.
explanations.american-revolutionary-war--inconfidenci: The Inconfidência's own article, which this atlas already cites for the record, opens by naming its cause in so many words: **"It was the result of a confluence of external and internal causes. The external inspiration was the independence of thirteen British colonies in North America following the American Revolutionary War"**. The article says inspiration and the atlas has a type for that, so `inspired` is the type and not `caused`: the sentence puts the internal causes beside the external one and does not rank them. Probable, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is.
explanations.american-revolutionary-war--treaty-of-pa: The treaty's own article opens by naming what it was: **"The Treaty of Paris, signed by representatives of King George III of Great Britain and representatives of the United States on September 3, 1783, officially ended the War of American Independence and recognized the Thirteen Colonies … to be free, sovereign, and independent unified states."** The war's own article says the same from the other end — the victory at Yorktown **"led King George III and the Kingdom of Great Britain to negotiate an end to the war"** (revision 1376266742). A settlement that a war is negotiated into is caused by it, so the type is `caused`; `probable`, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is. The treaty is also *part of* the war here, which is a display fact and not an argument — `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so this edge is what puts the treaty in the graph at all.
explanations.battle-of-pillpinto--siege-of-cusco-1781: Two sentences of the article, and the edge is no wider than what stands between them. The first groups this battle with two others as the victories the rising's first phase turned on: **"This initial phase of the rebellion in Cusco and the south was marked by key victories, such as the capture of Ayaviri, the Battle of Pillpinto, and especially the Battle of Sangarará, which consolidated rebel control over the Cusco region."** The second gives the offensive against Cusco as the attempt to keep what had been won: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** **The second sentence does not name Pillpinto**, and this record says so rather than reading it in: what the article supports is that Pillpinto is one of the victories that made the position the offensive set out from, which is `enabled` at `probable` and nothing stronger. Pillpinto's own article adds what was held there — "a small women's brigade led by Tomasa Tito Condemayta successfully suppressing the Spanish militia from capturing Túpac Amaru II" (revision 1370586073).
explanations.battle-of-sangarara--siege-of-cusco-1781: The rebellion's article, opening its "Siege of Cusco" section, gives the march on the city as a decision taken to hold what had been won: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** The sentences on either side put the same thing in order — Túpac Amaru returned to Tungasuca on 17 December, "the rebel leader began preparations for the great expedition against Cusco", and the army departed on 20 December. `enabled` and not `caused`, because Sangarará is one of three advantages the sentence names and the article gives no weight to any of them; what the source supports is that the victory was part of the position from which the offensive was launched, and not that it brought the offensive about.
explanations.battle-of-saylla--siege-of-cusco-1781--p: The article puts the two engagements two days apart and in one sequence: the reinforcements under Avilés entered Cusco on 1 January 1781, then **"On 2 January, alerted by the priest of Urcos, the cavalry of the Royalists, commanded by Joaquín de Varcárcel and Francisco Laisequilla, destroyed Castelo's vanguard in the town of Saylla, killing 400 rebels and capturing a flag bearing the coat of arms of Túpac Amaru"**, and then **"On 4 January, Túpac Amaru ordered his troops to move around the city"**, which is where the siege begins. **The article gives the order and the position and states no cause between them**, which is why the type is the weakest one the arrangement supports and the confidence is `probable`: the royalist cavalry had broken the rebel vanguard outside the city before the main army reached it, and that is the whole of what is claimed here. (Saylla's own article dates the action 3 January; the rebellion's dates it 2 January. Neither is preferred here and the record keeps its item's own date.)
explanations.capture-of-ayaviri--siege-of-cusco-1781-: The same two sentences, on the same reading and with the same limit. The article names the capture among the first phase's key victories — **"such as the capture of Ayaviri, the Battle of Pillpinto, and especially the Battle of Sangarará, which consolidated rebel control over the Cusco region"** — and gives the march on Cusco as the move to hold the advantages gained: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** **Ayaviri is not among the three that second sentence names either.** Ayaviri's own article says what the town was taken for — "part of Túpac Amaru II's plan to expand in the Lake Titicaca and possibly unite with the rebels in Charcas" (revision 1370608267) — which is a plan and points south rather than at Cusco, and is quoted here rather than made into an edge of its own. `enabled` at `probable`, for the same reason as Pillpinto.
explanations.execution-of-louis-xvi--insurrection-of-: The insurrection’s lead says what the deputies were attacked for: “Jean-Paul Marat led the attack on the representatives in the National Convention, who in January had voted against the execution of King Louis XVI and since then had paralyzed the convention.” The vote of January 1793 is the execution this atlas holds as a record, and the article gives it as the mark against the twenty-two Girondins the Commune demanded be brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal. So the later event is a reaction to the earlier one in the article’s own telling, which is what `reacted-to` says; the edge runs from the execution to the insurrection because that is the direction this atlas writes a reaction in. `probable`: the lead reports the grievance, it does not argue the causation, and rule 22 refuses `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation.
explanations.flight-to-varennes--champ-de-mars-massac: The massacre’s own lead lays the sequence out in three sentences and in this order: “two days before, the National Constituent Assembly issued a decree that King Louis XVI would retain his throne under a constitutional monarchy. This decision came after Louis and his family had unsuccessfully tried to flee France in the Flight to Varennes the month before. Later that day, leaders of the republicans in France rallied against this decision.” The article therefore makes the flight the thing the decree answered and the decree the thing the crowd came out against; what it does not say is that the flight caused the killing, and the type is `precondition-of` rather than `caused` for exactly that reason — the decree stands between them and this atlas does not hold it as a record. `probable`, on one encyclopaedia lead.
explanations.french-revolution--haitian-revolution-17: The English article states the link in its own words under "Lasting change": "The Enlightenment ideals and the initiation of the French Revolution were enough to inspire the Haitian Revolution, which evolved into the most successful and comprehensive slave rebellion in history", and in the sentence before it, "The call for modification of society was influenced by the revolution in France, but once the hope for change found a place in the hearts of the Haitian people, there was no stopping the radical reformation that was occurring." The section "Effects of the French Revolution" carries the same claim in detail: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen "declar[ed] all men free and equal" and was "ambiguous as to whether this equality applied to women, slaves, or citizens of the colonies, and thus influenced the desire for freedom and equality in Saint-Domingue." The type is `inspired` because that is the verb the article uses and the limit of what it asserts: the same section says "The Revolution in Haiti did not wait on the Revolution in France", which is the article refusing the stronger claim. Probable, because the warrant is Wikipedia and not a historian's argument; Wikidata carries no causal statement between Q6534 and Q689128 at all, so this edge has one author where the rest of this branch's have two.
explanations.french-revolution--napoleonic-wars--enab: The article on the Napoleonic Wars opens by saying where they came from: **"The wars originated in political forces arising from the French Revolution (1789–1799) and French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802) and produced a period of French domination over continental Europe."** Originating in political forces arising from a revolution is enabling and not causing — the sentence names no act of the revolution that set a war going — and the weaker of the two types the source allows is the one written. The same lead lists the Peninsular War among the seven conflicts the Napoleonic Wars are made of, which is why that war is filed under this one rather than linked to it. Probable, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is.
explanations.haitian-revolution-1791-1804--the-cuban-: The cited account is direct: after the end of slavery in Saint-Domingue at the turn of the nineteenth century, with the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became the most substantial sugar plantation colony in the Caribbean, outperforming the British islands. The richest producer in the world stopped producing and the market went to the island next to it. The revolution’s second effect on Cuba runs the other way and is in the same sources: the white upper class was so afraid of following Haiti that it supported Spanish rule intensely, which is part of why Cuba was still a slave colony of Spain when its neighbours had been republics for two generations.
explanations.rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii--siege-of-cu: The article gives the march on Cusco as a move the rising made out of its own position, and gives the reason in one sentence: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** The sentence before it says what he was anticipating — **"Túpac Amaru had received news of an impending attack on Tinta, which was why he quickly returned to Tungasuca"** — and the one after it that "the rebel leader began preparations for the great expedition against Cusco", the army departing on 20 December with some five thousand armed men. This is an edge from an umbrella to one of its own parts, written because `parent` is a display fact that never enters the adjacency: the three months of rising that put an army outside Cusco are the argument, and without this edge the graph could not walk it. `enabled` and not `caused`: the article gives the decision to Túpac Amaru and a warning about Tinta, not to the rising as such. Walker is the work the article itself cites through this stretch; it is cited and not read, which is why the confidence stays `probable`.
explanations.rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii--spanish-ame: The wars' article, under "Background", names this rising among the revolts the Bourbon reforms provoked: **"In other areas, the changes in the crown's economic and administrative policies led to tensions with locals, which at times erupted into open revolts, such as the Revolt of the Comuneros in New Granada and the Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in Peru."** The next paragraph is what this edge is drawn from and it is equivocal, so it is quoted whole: **"The loss of high offices to peninsulars and the eighteenth-century revolts in Spanish South America were some of the direct causes of the wars of independence, which took place decades later, but they have been considered important elements of the political background in which the wars took place."** `precondition-of` is the weakest type that sentence supports, and `caused` is not written from a sentence that hedges itself in its own second clause. The paragraph cites Lynch, Rodríguez and Kinsbruner; the one the article gives in full is cited here beside it, and it is cited and not read, which is why the confidence stays probable.
explanations.revolt-of-the-comuneros-new-granada--spa: The same paragraph of the wars' article that names the Túpac Amaru rising names this one in the same breath — **"open revolts, such as the Revolt of the Comuneros in New Granada and the Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in Peru"** — and the same hedged sentence follows it: **"The loss of high offices to peninsulars and the eighteenth-century revolts in Spanish South America were some of the direct causes of the wars of independence, which took place decades later, but they have been considered important elements of the political background in which the wars took place."** The revolt's own article gives the grievance: the rising was "in reaction to the increase in taxation to raise funds for the defense of the region against the British and a rise in the price of tobacco and brandy", which "were part of the late eighteenth-century Bourbon Reforms" (revision 1369393858). `precondition-of` for the same reason as its twin, and probable for the same reason.
explanations.siege-of-cusco-1781--battle-of-pucacasa-: The siege's article says what the failed siege left behind: **"Following the rebel retreat, momentum of the rebels slowed down and royalists in Cusco celebrated"**, and **"The final, larger and professional group of reinforcements of Lima arrived in Cusco on 24 February 1781, with a count of over 20,000."** The rebellion's article takes it from there — **"The royalists took the offensive, now having an advantage in armament and cavalry"** — and Pucacasa is where that offensive first met the main rebel army: its own article calls it **"the first major engagement between the Spanish reinforcements from Lima and Túpac Amaru's main army"** (revision 1370586703). `enabled` and not `caused`: the reinforcements had been sent for before the siege ended and the article does not make the siege's failure the reason for the march, only the state of the war the march set out into. Walker is the work the article itself cites for the march on Tinta and the ruse that ended at Pucacasa; it is cited here and not read, which is why the confidence stays `probable`.
explanations.storming-of-the-bastille--french-revolut: The article ends its lead with the claim outright: the fall of the Bastille “was the flashpoint of the French Revolution”. The same lead is careful about what the fortress actually was — a prison holding seven inmates and already scheduled for demolition — and rests the claim on what it stood for rather than on what was taken: “at the time, the Bastille represented royal authority in the centre of Paris”. That is an argument about a symbol becoming an act, which is what `caused` says here, and it is the same shape this atlas already gives a war’s opening action: the Bohemian revolt and the Thirty Years’ War, the Moncada attack and the Cuban Revolution. It stays `probable`: an encyclopaedia lead reporting where the consensus sits is not a work arguing it, and rule 22 refuses `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation in any case. The storming is also filed as part of the revolution, and that is a separate statement — `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so the argument has to be made as an edge or not at all.
explanations.the-british-industrial-revolution--slave: The other half of the Williams argument, and the one his critics attacked hardest: that it was the rise of industrial capitalism in Britain that destroyed the slave trade, the West Indian interest having become an obstacle to a manufacturing economy rather than its engine. The Act of 1807 is where that claim is tested, and the cited account of Capitalism and Slavery says Williams wrote it against a historiography that used the abolition acts as a moral pivot. The atlas records the claim as disputed because the dissent is at least as well argued as the thesis.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--cuban-revolution--: The cited account of the revolution names five socioeconomic problems that marked the decade before it, and three of them are this record’s: excessive dependence on sugar cultivation and exports, reliance on the United States for investment and trade, and a low rate of growth. The sugar sector was subject to American quotas and to world prices, it was seasonal and so dragged trade and transport with it, and Cuban capital went into real estate and financial investments in the United States rather than into industry at home. A hundred and sixty-eight years separate the two records and the type is the weak one: the monoculture is what the revolution happened inside, not what made it.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--cuban-war-of-indep: Abolition in 1886 broke the arrangement that had held Cuba to Spain. The freedmen went into the countryside and the towns; the economy could not carry the speed of the reform; wealthy Cubans lost property and fell into the middle class; the mills consolidated into the hands of companies and the largest owners, increasingly American ones. By 1894 ninety per cent of Cuban exports went to the United States and Cuba’s exports to Spain were a twelfth of that. A colony whose commerce had stopped running through its metropole, with a dispossessed creole class in it, is the one that rose in 1895.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--platt-amendment-19: What the settlement of 1901 was written around is named in the sources on both sides of it. Theodore Roosevelt, arguing for the war: "Our own direct interests were great, because of the Cuban tobacco and sugar, and especially because of Cuba’s relation to the projected Isthmian Canal." Some historians read even the Teller Amendment’s ban on annexation as protection for American sugar-beet growers rather than for Cuban independence. And after Cuba accepted the Amendment the United States ratified a tariff giving Cuban sugar preference in the American market and protecting selected American goods in the Cuban one. The type is the weak one because the Amendment’s seven conditions are about troops, treaties and naval stations rather than about cane; the boom is the thing that made Cuba worth writing them about.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--spanish-american-w: The weakest type, and the sources are the reason it is not a stronger one. American money had been buying into the devalued Cuban sugar market since the Ten Years’ War, and by 1894 the United States held the economic power over Cuba while Spain held the political authority — that is the asymmetry the war resolved. But the sugar investors did not want the war. The cited account has them looking to Spain to restore order, and the shipping firms pressing Washington to end the revolt: stability, not war, was what both wanted. So this edge does not say the sugar interest procured the intervention. It says the intervention happened in a country the United States already owned the economy of, and that this is why intervening was thinkable.
explanations.transfer-of-the-colonial-capital-to-rio-: The court did not have to build a seat of government when it arrived, because one was standing. Rio had been the capital of the State of Brazil since 1763 and the king’s representative there had been styled Viceroy since then; from 1808 the same city held the government of the whole empire, which some historians call a metropolitan reversal. Forty-four years is a long precondition, and that is what the type says: without it the transfer would have been a different and much harder thing, but 1763 did not bring 1807 about.
explanations.treaty-of-madrid-13-january-1750--first-: The 1777 treaty is the 1750 one taken up again after it failed. The Treaty of Madrid article: "The terms of the Treaty of Madrid, with a few exceptions, were re-established in the First Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1777, and that treaty was again negated in 1801." The San Ildefonso article says the same from its own end, in its background: "The 1750 Treaty of Madrid sought to resolve the dispute, but it was annulled in 1761 by the new Spanish monarch Charles III", after which came the Fantastic War of 1762-1763, the Spanish capture of Colónia do Sacramento and its return under the Treaty of Paris of 1763. Twenty-seven years and a war separate them and the second settles what the first could not, so the first is a `precondition-of` the second and did not cause it. Probable, on two articles at one revision each.
explanations.treaty-of-madrid-13-january-1750--guaran: Both articles say it, each from its own end. The Treaty of Madrid article, under "Legacy": "The Treaty of Madrid was significant because it substantially defined the modern boundaries of Brazil. However, the resistance of the Jesuits to surrendering their missions, and the refusal of the Guaraní to be forcibly relocated, led to the nullification of the treaty by the subsequent Treaty of El Pardo, signed by both countries in 1761. The opposition by the Guaraní led to the Guaraní War of 1756." The Guaraní War article opens with the same sentence turned round: the war "was a result of the 1750 Treaty of Madrid, which set a line of demarcation between Spanish and Portuguese colonial territory in South America." A treaty that moved a line across seven missions and ordered the people living in them to leave, and a war fought by those people against the two crowns that signed it, is causation and not a shared background, so `caused`. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading.
explanations.united-states-declaration-of-independenc: The two articles describe one claim and its recognition seven years apart. The Declaration **"explains why the Thirteen Colonies regarded themselves as independent sovereign states no longer subject to British colonial rule"**; the treaty **"recognized the Thirteen Colonies, which had been part of colonial British America, to be free, sovereign, and independent unified states."** Neither article says the second followed from the first, and this edge does not say so either: it takes `precondition-of`, the weakest of the five, for a claim that had to exist before it could be recognised in the same words. `probable`.
explanations.war-of-jenkins-ear--battle-of-cartagena-: The battle is an operation of the war, and the war is what put a British fleet in the Caribbean for it. The Battle of Cartagena de Indias article opens: "The Battle of Cartagena de Indias took place during the 1739 to 1748 War of Jenkins’ Ear between Spain and Great Britain. The result of long-standing commercial tensions, the war was primarily fought in the Caribbean; the British tried to capture key Spanish ports in the region, including Porto Bello and Chagres in Panama, Havana, and Cartagena de Indias in present-day Colombia." The War of Jenkins’ Ear article names it in the same terms: "The most significant operation of the war was a failed British attack on Cartagena in 1741, which resulted in heavy casualties and ship losses, and was not repeated." A war that sends the fleet does not cause any one of its engagements, which is why this is `enabled` and not `caused`; that the battle is also part of the war is said by `parent` and not by this edge. Probable, on two articles at one revision each.
explanations.war-of-jenkins-ear--war-of-the-austrian-: The mechanism is in the Battle of Cartagena de Indias article, under "Aftermath", about the defeat that ended this war’s American campaign: "News of Britain’s defeat reached Europe at the end of June 1741 and had immense repercussions. It caused George II of Great Britain, who had been acting as mediator between Frederick the Great of Prussia and Maria Theresa supporting Austria over Prussian seizure of Silesia in December 1740, to withdraw Britain’s guarantees of armed support for the Pragmatic Sanction. That encouraged France and Spain, the Bourbon allies, revealed to also be allied with Prussia, to move militarily against a now isolated Austria." The reading is attributed there to Reed Browning, The War of the Austrian Succession (1993), pp. 58-66. The War of the Austrian Succession article names this war among its own from its first paragraph: "Related conflicts include King George’s War, the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the First Carnatic War, and the First and Second Silesian Wars." The wider war is dated from the Prussian invasion of Silesia in December 1740, a year after this one began and six months before the news from Cartagena reached Europe, so this war cannot have caused it: what it did was take away the guarantee that had held Britain between the two sides, which is `enabled`. Probable and not consensus: the work is named in the article rather than read here (A2).
